title: The Japanese philosophy that could save us from AI
subtitle: AI, ikigai, and the Japanese secret to meaning in life
author: Ken Mogi
introduction: AI researchers warn AI could take our jobs, replace creatives, and even take away the sense that our lives have meaning. Japanese scientist Ken Mogi, argues that the Japanese philosophy of ikigai can help overcome these threats from AI. Ikigai, which Mogi argues is wrongly translated as "purpose in life", has entered the global conversation with best-selling books highlighting the connection between ikigai and well-being, and even life expectancy. By escaping the idea that meaning in life is measurable or based on productivity, ikigai could prevent the AI we build from falling into that same trap.
body:
In recent years, the Japanese word ikigai has come to be widely known in the world. Typically translated as purpose of life, ikigai is deeply embedded in the life of the Japanese people. I have written a book on ikigai in 2017, and it has been translated into 32 languages and published in 58 countries. In Germany, my ikigai book became the no.1 bestselling non-fiction book of the year 2024.

Ikigai is known to be tightly associated with well-being. A landmark study conducted in Japan found significant correlations between ikigai and longer life expectancy. Today, there is interest in ikigai as a health-promoting principle, originally coming from the island nation of Japan, which boasts one of the longest life expectancies in the world, and is applicable to people everywhere.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The game of life With Slavoj Žižek, Steven Bonnell, Lisa Miller, Myriam François

Intriguingly, ikigai is now starting to have a significant impact on AI alignment. Ever since the so-called ChatGPT moment in 2023, people have been amazed and fascinated by the rapid development in AI. AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) and ASI (Artificial Superintelligence) are now discussed not only as fantastical hypotheses but also as practical research and development themes. Given the accelerating advances of AI, ikigai is emerging as a humanistic principle that could help us see where to go from here.

Purpose is a universal evaluator of many fields of human activities, and will certainly lead at least a part of artificial intelligence development from here.

In a Lex Fridman podcast, AI researcher Roman Yampolskiy discussed ikigai risk, the potentially detrimental effect of AI development on people's mental welfare, in terms of depriving their sense of ikigai. The ikigai risk could turn out to be even more dangerous than things like losing jobs due to AI. Loss of ikigai would cut more close to the heart than job loss, and lead to a fundamental deterioration of the human experience. On the other hand, there could be ways to enhance people's sense of ikigai through the use of artificial intelligence, by letting people focus on things that would give them ikigai in their professional and private lives, while delegating ikigai-less chores to AI.

In order to understand the fundamentals of AI alignment regarding ikigai, we need to go back to some basic principles regarding how artificial intelligence systems are configured. In the reinforcement learning essential to the training of AI, some criteria based on evaluation functions are set to fine-tune and configure the weights in the network. For example, AI of games such as chess, shogi, and Go are trained in such ways that the moves chosen will be likely to lead to a win. Large Language Models are trained in such a manner that text generated by the next token prediction algorithms is optimal from the viewpoint of human natural language. In general, AI is great in optimization, where the evaluation function would tell you what kind of modifications are necessary to make the system more likely to generate results closer to the optimum.

Admiring flowers in your garden can be your ikigai but the world doesn't necessarily need it.

AI is a mirror of the human condition. Human behavior can also be assessed through some evaluation functions, constrained by evolutionary principles, which, biologically, will be reflected in the number of offspring each of us would reproduce and successfully raise. Human activities can also be evaluated by social and cultural impacts, by how each of us would be remembered, both professionally and privately. Peter Drucker made the famous statement that the purpose of a business is to create and keep customers. Purpose is a universal evaluator of many fields of human activities, and will certainly lead at least a part of artificial intelligence development from here. For example, the purpose of a chess AI is to win. The purpose of AlphaFold is to predict the three-dimensional structure of proteins given the sequence of amino acids. The purpose of generative AI is to generate outputs that would be satisfactory for humans. When giving the prompt "generate a Studio Ghibli-style image from this photo", humans expect an output with certain qualities, in line with works from the famous anime studio.

In order to get down to the essence of ikigai, we need to start with some clarifications. Ikigai is interesting because its role is different from purpose. In popular culture, there are several misconceptions about ikigai. For example, a widely circulated Venn diagram of ikigai depicts it as a cross-section of ‘what you love’, ‘what the world needs’, ‘what you can be paid for’ and ‘what you are good at’. This would appropriately describe a purpose in business or life, but not ikigai. ‘What you love’ would certainly be a necessary condition for ikigai. The other three conditions are irrelevant.

In general, ikigai can be something personal that does not necessarily align with what is valued in the world.

Admiring flowers in your garden can be your ikigai but the world doesn't necessarily need it. You wouldn't necessarily be paid for your ikigai of painting. You might find a great joy in singing, while being not at all good at it, as exemplified by Madame Florence.

In general, ikigai can be something personal that does not necessarily align with what is valued in the world. In my case, I have ikigai in watching butterflies fly around as I go for a run in Tokyo, a legacy from my childhood interests in these tiny creatures. (For the record, I have never been paid for my love of butterflies, except for a modest fee for a talk I once gave to butterfly lovers in Japan.) Ikigai thus is distinct from purpose, in that the former can be described in terms of evaluation functions such as money and social recognition, while the latter cannot be treated that way.

Theoretically, ikigai could play an interesting and significant role in AI alignment because of its neutrality to evaluation functions, while being central to life itself. Ikigai is crucial in maintaining our physical and mental well-being in a time of rapid changes. The current zeitgeist centered on meritocracy means that each of us is acutely sensitive about our brownie points. The development of AI is pursued along this line, in which everything is assessed and given a nod from the functionalist master, or even a Moloch. AI development would perhaps lead to an efficiently managed civilization in the best-case scenario, but our heart and fundamental conditions for healthy life might lie elsewhere.

I once had the fascinating experience of interviewing Hayao Miyazaki, famous for such works as My Neighbor Totoro and Spirited Away. Over the course of making a film, Miyazaki has to draw hundreds of storyboards, a job the renowned anime master does with ikigai, blissfully unaware of the potential social rewards, such as an Academy Award or the box office. The practical considerations are left to the discretion of the Studio Ghibli producer Toshio Suzuki. Miyazaki's labor of ikigai is reflected in the quality of the work. Moments when the wandering soot (makkuro kurosuke), catbus, or the eponymous Totoro troll appear in My Neighbor Totoro, the viewers feel such profound joys precisely because Miyazaki produced them with ikigai.

In human cognition, ikigai correlates with the state of flow, in which one forgets the passage of time and finds joy in what one is doing, without reference to external rewards.

In general, things created with ikigai tend to give people tremendous inner pleasure. Indeed, ikigai would be one of the primary venues for empathy and transmission of love. This is understandable, as shared ikigai would have been great in building community and making human cognition and behavior robust in the history of human evolution.

Ikigai as a mother of quality in creative works raises important challenges for the development of generative AI. In the current flood of AI-generated texts, images, and videos, do we find genuinely valuable works? Is a Studio Ghibli-style image equivalent to a scene from an actual Hayao Miyazaki film? Can generative AI pass the ikigai version of the Turing test?

In human cognition, ikigai correlates with the state of flow, in which one forgets the passage of time and finds joy in what one is doing, without reference to external rewards. Ikigai is central to the homeostasis of the mind-body that support robust choice and behavior. Ikigai is also related to the secure base and attachment, described by the British psychologist John Bowlby and American-Canadian psychologist Mary Ainsworth, that humans need to have in order to explore the unknown.

A division of labor will be important in the alignment of humans and AI. Artificial intelligence systems excel in the business of optimization. Humans are capable of finding the best solution for important problems, but do not necessarily enjoy the job. With the pressure of competition in a globalizing economy, perhaps humans desire at least a partial and temporary release from the burden of optimization, to reclaim secure base and attachment.

In order to optimize, statistical analysis of big data is necessary, just as generative AI such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok are doing on the strength of data provided by humans over the years. Recently, there is the worrying trend of AI slop, with low quality contents generated by AI increasingly dominating the internet. As platforms give monetary reward based on social media metrics such as views, impressions, and engagements, content farms feeding brain rots have become the norm rather than exceptions. This rather trivial and empty success in content optimization under current evaluation functions is symbolic of the general limits and vulnerabilities of AI. We do need to keep humans in the loop here, so that the cyberspace wouldn't deteriorate into an AI echo-chamber dystopia.

Ikigai, where humans find the joy of being alive while absorbed in the here and now, can serve as the ultimate guardian of quality in AI alignment, and an antidote for the pathology of self-serving AI minions. By exploring how ikigai could be enhanced by AI, the ikigai risk could be turned into an ikigai opportunity. For now, ikigai is a human phenomenon, but there is no reason why it should not be applied to artificial intelligence systems as well. Someday, even artificial ikigai could be built, a theme, a premonition for which is found in Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun. Understanding how to create artificial ikigai would contribute to the construction of robust AI agents aligned with safety, and might ultimately lead to a genuine understanding of conditions for artificial and natural consciousness, as ikigai and consciousness together are central to what we humans are.
